name: Salonul de proiecte
overview: Research and production programme for contemporary art in Palatul Universul, Corp B, first floor, Actor Ion Brezoianu 23-25, Bucharest. It promotes Romanian contemporary art through exhibitions, publications, presentations and debates, in dialogue with the regional and international context (stated by the space).
Founded in 2011 in the framework of MNAC Anexa. Since 2016 it has functioned as an independent art space in Palatul Universul. Organised by the non-profit Asociația Salonul de proiecte.
Team: Alexandra Croitoru, Magda Radu, Ștefan Sava and Ana-Maria Ștefan.
funding_verdict: Salonul de proiecte (Bucharest): mixed public and private project funding: Romania's national cultural fund, foundations, a bank and small sponsors

name: tranzit.ro
overview: Romanian non-governmental organisation for contemporary art, "initiated and funded by ERSTE Foundation", announced on 15 December 2011 and fully active from early 2012 (e-flux).

A closed call chose five people to run it: Matei Bejenaru, Livia Pancu, Lia Perjovschi, Attila Tordai-S and Raluca Voinea (e-flux). Temporary Art Review (2017) named Voinea as director of tranzit.ro Bucharest.
It is the fifth member of the tranzit.org network, founded in 2002, with associations in Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia; each operates autonomously (e-flux; ERSTE Foundation).
funding_verdict: tranzit.ro: foundation-funded: ERSTE Foundation, with Romanian state project grants

name: Rwanda Art Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum in Kanombe, in the Nyarugunga sector of Kicukiro district, about four kilometres east of Kigali airport (Wikipedia, KT Press, The New Times).
The villa opened to the public in February 2009 as the Presidential Palace Museum. It was renamed the Rwanda Art Museum on 18 May 2018, International Museum Day (Wikipedia, The New Times).
Not named for a person: the building was the residence of President Juvénal Habyarimana until 1994 and later of President Pasteur Bizimungu (The New Times, KT Press).
funding_verdict: Rwanda Art Museum: public: Rwandan state body
wider_context: Wrong argues the government-run museums anchor the regime's legacy "in brick and mortar" and present a selective view of Rwandan history (Foreign Policy, 2016).
The Academy that runs the Rwanda Art Museum runs the national museums, and the building is the former presidential villa, then the Presidential Palace Museum, that Wrong describes.

press_items.title: Michela Wrong, "The False Idols of Rwanda's Genocide" (2016)
Jonathan W. Rosen, "In Rwanda, a Tour of Disaster" (2014)

name: Kër Thiossane
overview: Villa for art and multimedia in the Sicap neighbourhood of Dakar, run as a Senegalese non-governmental association (Pixelache, 2010; Agenda 21 for Culture). A 2024 listing gives the address as Villa N 1695, Sicap Liberté 2 (au-senegal.com).

Activities began in 2002. Pixelache names Marion Louisgrand-Sylla and François Sylla as founders. The Daniel Langlois Foundation says it was initiated by Momar François Sylla, an artist and musician, and that it officially opened in September 2003.
Sylla grew up in the villa and wanted a space rooted in the Sicap neighbourhood. Louisgrand-Sylla had worked in Paris at Mains d'Oeuvres (Pixelache).
funding_verdict: Kër Thiossane: project-funded: small association living on grants from the Daniel Langlois Foundation and the EU's ACP Cultures programme

name: Musée Boribana
overview: Museum of contemporary African art in Dakar, at the Rond-point Place ONU, Boulevard Dial Diop at Boulevard du Canal 4 (Senegalese culture ministry page).
Founded by the Senegalese anthropologist Boubacar Koné, who has since died, and his wife, the actress CCH Pounder (culture ministry page; DakArtNews, 6 July 2026).
Sources give different founding years: 1990 (culture ministry), 1992 (DakArtNews) and 1998 (Enquête+, 2015); French Wikipedia gives both 1998 and 1990.
funding_verdict: Musée Boribana: state-owned since December 2014; built with the founders' private money

press_items.title: Remy Mallet, "She Helped Build Senegal's First Private Museum of Contemporary Art. Today, CCH Pounder Collects 'for the Future'" (2026)

name: Center for Cultural Decontamination (CZKD)
overview: Independent non-profit cultural centre in the Veljković Pavilion at Birčaninova 21, Belgrade, known as "Kod Borke" after its founder (Radio Slobodna Evropa, 2010).
Founded in 1994 by Borka Pavićević, formerly a principal of the Yugoslav Drama Theatre (Wikipedia); it began work at noon on 1 January 1995 with the "First Decontamination" (Vreme, 2025; CZKD).
Vreme calls it the oldest anti-war centre in Serbia; the centre describes itself as an institution of critical thinking set up against nationalism, xenophobia and violence (CZKD).
funding_verdict: CZKD: grant-funded: foreign foundations, notably the Mott Foundation and the Sigrid Rausing Trust

press_items.title: Olja Bećković, interview with Ranko Munitić (2005)

name: Post-Museum
overview: Independent cultural and social space in Singapore that describes itself as an open platform for examining contemporary life, promoting the arts and connecting people (Post-Museum site).
Founded in 2007 by the husband-and-wife artist-activists Jennifer Teo and Woon Tien Wei (On Curating interview; Artshelp).

From 2007 to 2011 it ran a physical space in two shophouses on Rowell Road in the Kampong Kapur area. It has operated nomadically since, holding events in different venues (On Curating; Post-Museum site).
funding_verdict: Post-Museum: independent: no government funding in its early years, according to the founders

name: Plečnik House
overview: Museum in the former home of the architect Jože Plečnik at Karunova 4 to 6 in Trnovo, Ljubljana. It has been a monument of national importance since 2009 (museum site).
A public museum since 1974, it was renovated from 2013 and reopened in 2015. The Museum and Galleries of Ljubljana (MGML) runs it (European Heritage Awards).
Named for Plečnik. The museum says many of his ideas for Ljubljana were conceived in the house (museum site).
funding_verdict: Plečnik House: public: the City of Ljubljana and the Ministry of Culture, through MGML

name: Norval Foundation
overview: Art museum and sculpture garden at 4 Steenberg Road, Tokai, Cape Town, showing modern and contemporary art from the African continent and its diaspora, between mountains and wetlands (norvalfoundation.org).

Founded by the property investor Louis Norval, who chairs the board of trustees. The Art Newspaper (26 April 2018) gave 28 April 2018 as the opening date, seven months after Zeitz MOCAA, and the Sunday Independent (4 May 2018) describes the opening after a Freedom Day preview. Norval bought a plot of nearly 12 acres in 2011.
Core holding: the Homestead Art Collection of 20th-century South African art, which the Norval family assembled over about two decades (Sunday Independent, 2018).
funding_verdict: Norval Foundation: privately funded: founder Louis Norval's money, plus a capital fund, income schemes and sponsors

name: Bag Factory Artists' Studios
overview: Artists' studios, gallery and residency programme at 10 Mahlathini Street, Newtown, Johannesburg, on the border of Fordsburg and Newtown, next to the Oriental Plaza and close to Newtown Junction (stated by the organisation).

Founded in 1991 as Fordsburg Artists' Studios, trading as Bag Factory Artists' Studios, by Dr David Koloane, the British philanthropist Robert Loder and the arts administrator Sandra (Sandy) Burnett (Contemporary And). The Mail & Guardian reported in 1995 that the studios opened in the disused Speedy Bag Factory early in 1991, as workspace for artists linked to Thupelo, and placed them in Fordsburg.
Named for its first home, the disused Speedy Bag Factory. The Mail & Guardian reported the retrospective "The Speedy Bag Factory: The First Four Years" at the Civic Gallery in 1995.
funding_verdict: Bag Factory Artists' Studios: no funders named: studio rents, residency fees and unnamed international partners

press_items.title: Ian Tromp, "Of rat traps and art prats" (1995)

name: Art Sonje Center
overview: Private contemporary art centre at 87 Yulgok-ro 3-gil, Jongno-gu, east of Gwanghwamun Gate, near Anguk station (centre website). Wikipedia places it in Samcheong-dong.

Opened in 1998, after the "Sprout" (싹) exhibitions of 1995 in a hanok and a Western-style house on the site. Founder and chair Heeja K. Chung (정희자) set it up to remember her late son, Kim Son-je, after founding the Sonje Museum of Art in Gyeongju in 1991 (centre website).

Building: three floors and a basement by the architect Kim Jong-sung (김종성), on a corner once occupied by a hanok; galleries of 219, 456 and 466 square metres, a 238-seat basement Art Hall, an inner garden and a rooftop garden (centre website).
funding_verdict: Art Sonje Center: private non-profit, founded by the Chung family as an extension of the Daewoo Foundation's arts work, with corporate partners and co-organisers
wider_context: On 30 May 2006 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Kim Woo-choong, Daewoo's founder and former chairman, to 10 years in prison, forfeiture of more than 21 trillion won and a 10 million won fine, for over 20 trillion won of accounting fraud, 9.8 trillion won of illegal financing, 19 trillion won diverted abroad and $100 million embezzled (AP via NBC News).
Daewoo collapsed under its debts after the 1997 to 1998 Asian financial crisis (AP via NBC News).
Kim was the main funder of the Daewoo Foundation, whose arts work the centre says it extends, and was married to its founder.

press_items.title: Ian Tee, "Editor's Notes: Exhibitions in Seoul" (2026)

name: Casa Bloc Museum-Apartment
overview: Dwelling 1/11, a 60 square metre duplex on the first floor of block 2 of the Casa Bloc social-housing complex in Sant Andreu, at Carrer de l'Almirall Pròixida on the corner of Passeig de Torras i Bages (Catalan Wikipedia; Disseny Hub).

The republican Generalitat's Institut Contra l'Atur Forçós commissioned Casa Bloc in 1932 from the GATCPAC architects Josep Lluís Sert, Josep Torres Clavé and Joan Baptista Subirana; President Francesc Macià laid the first stone in March 1933 (Catalan Wikipedia).

Five seven-storey blocks in an inverted "S". Work stopped in the civil war; the Diputació de Barcelona took over the complex and the Franco regime finished it, housing military families, war orphans and widows in its more than 200 flats. It returned to the Generalitat with democracy and was declared a Bé Cultural d'Interès Nacional in 1992 (Catalan Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Casa Bloc Museum-Apartment: public: Barcelona City Council through the Museu del Disseny, and the Generalitat's land institute INCASÒL

name: Hangar.org
overview: Centre for artistic production and research at c/ Emilia Coranty 16 (formerly Passatge Marquès de Sta. Isabel 40), in the Can Ricart complex in Poblenou, Barcelona (Barcelona City Council, Fàbriques de Creació).
Founded in 1997 by the Associació d'Artistes Visuals de Catalunya (AAVC). It has had private foundation status since 2003 (Barcelona City Council).

Building: an industrial warehouse in Can Ricart, a textile factory dating to 1853 by the architects Josep Oriol i Bernadet and Josep Fontserè i Mestres. The page credits Yaiza Alonso and Arantxa Manrique with the architecture project. It covers 2,600 square metres.
funding_verdict: Hangar: public and private support, with no funder list published: city hall paid its early rent and renovated its buildings, and a bank foundation co-ran a 2020 grant

press_items.title: Jeffrey Swartz, "Space-Run Artists: Art Activism and Urban Conflict in Contemporary Barcelona" (2008)

name: La Virreina Centre de la Imatge
overview: Publicly owned centre for contemporary art and the image in the Palau de la Virreina, La Rambla 99, which it describes as "effectively a passageway into the Raval neighbourhood" (La Virreina website).
Its stated programme runs along three lines, the city, the archive and images, through exhibitions, seminars, courses and publications (La Virreina website, mission page).

Named for the palace, which took its name from the viceroy's widow, Maria Francesca de Fivaller-Clasquerí i de Bru, who lived there after the death of her husband Manuel d'Amat, Viceroy of Peru, in 1782 (Catalan Wikipedia; Amics de la Rambla).
funding_verdict: La Virreina Centre de la Imatge: public: Barcelona City Council through its Institut de Cultura (ICUB)

name: MUHBA Bon Pastor
overview: Museum space in the Bon Pastor neighbourhood of the Sant Andreu district, at C/ Barnola 22, in a block of working-class "cheap houses" (cases barates). Part of the Barcelona History Museum (MUHBA) (museum site).

The block was one of four housing estates built in Barcelona in 1929 and has sixteen houses, ten of them now museum spaces. The project began in 2010 at the initiative of the neighbours' association AVV Bon Pastor (museum site).
Named for the neighbourhood. 3Cat says the Bon Pastor estate had 784 small houses without foundations and with damp problems (3Cat, 30 March 2019).
funding_verdict: MUHBA Bon Pastor: public: the Ajuntament de Barcelona through the Barcelona History Museum, with Neighbourhood Plan money for the new space
wider_context: The museum stands inside the demolition and rehousing of the Bon Pastor houses that the Patronat Municipal de l'Habitatge began in 2001. 3Cat (6 February 2022) reports that part of the residents opposed the demolition and kept demanding that it stop, that a 2003 referendum backed the remodelling, and that 215 of the 784 houses still stood.
3Cat (6 February 2022) quotes one 71-year-old resident who expects the family to gain in comfort in a new flat but says leaving the house stirs many feelings (my translation).
The link to the space: the museum occupies a preserved block of sixteen of the houses, and the neighbours' association started the project in 2010 (museum site).

name: Bulegoa z/b
overview: An "office for art and knowledge" at Solokoetxe 8 bajo, in the Solokoetxe district of Bilbao (stated by the space).

Full name "Bulegoa zenbaki barik" (Basque: "office without a number"; own translation). Founded in 2010 by Beatriz Cavia, Miren Jaio and Leire Vergara with Isabel de Naverán, who stayed until 2018; it marks its anniversary each November, the 16th in 2026 (stated by the space).

Team: the three founders, with Silvia Coppola on production and Auria Etxeandia on communication; advisers Elena Casado, Yaiza Hernández, Itziar Okariz, Ana Vujanović and the late Guadalupe Echevarría (1948 to 2023) (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: Bulegoa z/b: public: Basque, provincial, city, Spanish and EU culture funding, plus a New York foundation for one programme

name: Casa Broner
overview: Home and studio at Carreró de Sa Penya 15 in the sa Penya quarter of Eivissa (Ibiza Town), built in 1960 on the edge of a rock above the sea, over the remains of an older construction (MACE page; Arquitectura Viva).

Built by the German architect and painter Erwin Broner (Munich 1898 to Kreuth 1971), who was forced to emigrate because of his Jewish origins, reached Spain in 1933 and lived on Ibiza permanently from 1959 (MACE page; Illes Balears tourism page).
Named for Broner. It has been a Bé d'Interès Cultural since 2000 (MACE page).
funding_verdict: Casa Broner: public: the Ajuntament d'Eivissa, with Govern balear money for the restoration

name: Casa Masó
overview: House museum at Carrer de les Ballesteries 29 in Girona, whose rear façade faces the Onyar river (Fundació Rafael Masó site, Nació Digital).

Rafael Masó (1880 to 1935) was born in the house, which joins four houses the Masó family acquired between the mid-19th and early 20th centuries. It looks much as it did after his last renovation in 1919 and keeps its furniture and decoration (foundation site).

Named for Masó. The last owners, Narcís-Jordi Aragó Masó and Mercè Huerta Busquets, whom the foundation calls the architect's "nebots" (my translation: nephews), transferred it to the Ajuntament de Girona, which created the Fundació Rafael Masó in 2006 to manage it (foundation site).
funding_verdict: Casa Masó: public: the Ajuntament de Girona pays most of the foundation's budget

name: Museo Casa Botines Gaudí
overview: Gaudí's seven-storey building on Plaza San Marcelo in León, run as a museum by the Fundación Obra Social de Castilla y León (FUNDOS), whose seat is in the building (museum's site; FUNDOS accounts 2024).
Built 1891 to 1892 for the textile merchants Simón Fernández and Mariano Andrés as housing with a warehouse (English Wikipedia).
Named for Juan Homs y Botines, who opened a textile shop in León in 1834. Also called Casa Fernández y Andrés (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo Casa Botines Gaudí: foundation-run: FUNDOS, with a Junta de Castilla y León grant announced for 2026

name: Museo Sorolla
overview: A house museum at Paseo del General Martínez Campos 37, Madrid, in the house the Sorolla family lived in, with an extension building at Calle Zurbano 68 (Ministry of Culture museum page).

Clotilde García del Castillo's 1925 will left the house and collections to the Spanish State to create a museum in memory of her husband, the painter Joaquín Sorolla; the State accepted the bequest in 1931 and the museum opened in 1932 with its main floor open, was interrupted by the war and reopened in 1941 (Ministry of Culture museum page).
What is there: paintings, art objects and furniture from the house, plus later acquisitions; the page read gave no count of works (Ministry of Culture museum page).
funding_verdict: Museo Sorolla: public, a state museum run directly by the Ministry of Culture.
